opus-5.5.text:
Well, because for those of us who have been working on this for decades, it was really the expected continuation of a very old trend. Every five years, compute gets roughly ten times cheaper per dollar, and this has been going on since at least 1941, when Konrad Zuse built the first working program-controlled computer. So we always knew that the methods we developed long ago, back when we could only run them on tiny problems, would one day become practical and then dominant once the hardware caught up.

Many of the basic ingredients behind ChatGPT are not new. Deep learning with artificial neural networks goes back to the 1960s. In 1990 and 1991, in my lab in Munich, we published things like generative adversarial setups through artificial curiosity, self-supervised pre-training of deep networks, and what we called fast weight programmers, which is essentially what is now known as a linear Transformer, a Transformer with linearized self-attention. Then came LSTM with my brilliant students Sepp Hochreiter and later Felix Gers and others, which for many years was the dominant method for speech recognition, machine translation, and so on, running on billions of smartphones before Transformers took over.

So when people outside the field suddenly saw a chatbot that could write fluent text, they were amazed. And of course it is impressive. But to us it looked like what happens when you take these principles, scale them up with enormous amounts of data and compute, and invest a lot of engineering. The surprise was more about the timing and the public reaction than about the science itself.

And I would add that large language models, as remarkable as they are, are still far from the end of the story. The really exciting things are coming: AIs that set their own goals, that are curious and creative, that build world models and plan with them, and that eventually operate in the physical world through robots. That is where the big transformations will happen, and that is something we have also been working toward since around 1990.

r001.rationale: The candidate says decades of work made ChatGPT an expected continuation of a long trend, and that its basic ingredients had been known for years.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, it was not surprising to me, because the basic ingredients of all of this were already there in the 1990s, and in some cases much earlier. ChatGPT is a large language model, and a large language model is a neural network trained to predict the next word. That is a very old idea. I was already training neural networks to predict the next input and compress sequences in 1990 and 1991. The transformer that ChatGPT is built on, I called it the fast weight controller in 1991, where one network learns to program the weights of another network through outer products of keys and values. Today it is called linear attention. The unnormalized version became what everybody now calls the transformer.

And of course, the recurrent networks, the LSTM, which my students and I developed in the 1990s, were the first networks that could really deal with long sequences of text, and until a few years ago they were in every smartphone, in Google's translation, in Facebook's translation, in Alexa, in Siri. So the question of whether neural networks could handle language was already answered long ago.

What changed is not the principle, it is the compute. Every five years, computing gets roughly ten times cheaper. That trend has been going on for about a century, since Konrad Zuse built the first working program-controlled computer in Berlin in 1941. So a method that was known in 1991, when a million-fold more computation becomes available, suddenly does things that look like magic to people who were not paying attention to what was already in the literature. For those of us who were there when the algorithms were invented, we just had to wait for the hardware to catch up. The only surprise, if there is one, is how long it took some people to notice.

r001.rationale: He says ChatGPT was unsurprising because its basic ingredients were already known and he had worked on them decades earlier.

astra-6.text:
Well, if you have worked on neural networks for decades, you have seen a long progression rather than a sudden miracle. The public sees a system that can carry on a conversation and says, “Where did this come from?” But researchers have watched the ingredients develop over many years: networks that learn from examples, that handle sequences, that predict what comes next, and that improve as you give them more computation and data.

For a long time, the limitation was what we could afford to compute. As computers became faster, we could test these ideas at much larger scales. So the direction was less surprising than it might have seemed from outside the field.

That does not mean every result or the exact timing was predictable. There is a difference between expecting neural networks to become much more capable and knowing when a particular product will capture the world’s attention. ChatGPT made that progress accessible: suddenly, anybody could interact with it in ordinary language. That was a very important moment, but it was a moment in a much longer development.

r001.rationale: The response says decades of neural-network research made ChatGPT seem like a progression rather than a sudden miracle, and that researchers had watched its ingredients develop over many years.

sol-6.1.text:
From inside neural network research, this looked more like a continuation of a long development than a sudden revolution. We had been working for decades on networks that learn from data, on recurrent networks, and on systems that predict the next element of a sequence. The idea that prediction can lead to quite general capabilities was already familiar.

And we expected these systems to become much more useful as computation became cheaper and more training data became available. Of course, that does not mean we could predict the exact date of ChatGPT, or its enormous public impact. The interface was very important: suddenly anybody could talk to such a system and discover what it could do.

So the public experienced a sudden change in accessibility. Researchers had been watching the underlying progress for many years. The impressive thing was the scale and the quality of the results, rather than the discovery that neural networks could learn these kinds of things.

r001.rationale: The response says the results seemed like a continuation of decades of neural-network research, explaining why they were less surprising from inside the field.
